item.title: The Simons Observatory: A Novel Design for Heat Strap at Sub-Kelvin Temperatures
item.description: arXiv:2611.26698v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a novel process for the fabrication of copper heat straps and a measurement of their thermal performance at sub-Kelvin temperatures. The conductance of the heat straps is consistent with the bulk conductivity of annealed copper over the range 60 mK to 1 K. We find no evidence for deviation from a linear dependence of conductivity with temperature over the explored range, indicating that the contact resistance at the strap ends is sub-dominant. Heat straps developed and validated through the described process have been deployed in both the Large Aperture Telescope Receiver and a Small Aperture Telescope of the Simons Observatory and have met thermal requirements.
item.dc:creator: John Orlowski-Scherer, Oorie Desai, Daniel Lee, Nicholas Galitzki, Alex Manduca, Mark Devlin, Dominic Horne, Henry Nachman, Yuhan Wang, Edward J. Wollack

item.title: Chromatic calorimetry using nanocomposites: status and future challenges
item.description: arXiv:2611.27636v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The development of advanced detector technologies will play a key role in future high-energy physics experiments, such as the FCC-ee. In this context, chromatic calorimetry is an emerging concept for electromagnetic calorimeters, with the potential to combine the precise energy measurement of homogeneous calorimeters with longitudinal reconstruction of particle showers. The state of the art in chromatic calorimetry is reviewed, including experimental results from proof-of-concept prototypes and simulation studies investigating quantum-dot-based configurations. Recent progress and current challenges in the development of nanocomposites are also discussed. Finally, future prospects for chromatic calorimetry are outlined.

item.title: Passivity Correction of the Thermistor Model in Bolometric Power Sensors and Its Dependence on Bead Temperature
item.description: arXiv:2611.27744v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper closes a series of works on thermistor bolometric power sensors, coaxial and waveguide, by treating what the two have in common. The per-state transformation m introduced in the waveguide work, which corrects the thermistor impedances of the model in each bridge state so that the two-port of the mount is passive, is analyzed on the eleven sensors of the preceding papers: the corrections are a few tenths of a percent in the coaxial mounts and one to two percent in the waveguide mounts, follow one pattern within each family, and the hottest state is the one whose efficiency departs most from the others. The transformation is tested by an independent measurement: the substituted powers of the three states, read with the manufacturer's procedure against a leveled source whose reflection is obtained from the closure of three Apollonius circles, give efficiency ratios of 0.999 +/- 0.016 and 0.997 +/- 0.008 (k = 2), which contain the values at the passivity floor (0.996, 0.998) and exclude those of the first pass (0.941, 1.023). Three sensors were swept in the bridge resistance, 23 and 31 states, and a fourth is treated apart: the correction reduces to one constant per state, the parallel resistance of the bead, represented by a law with one term scaling with the bridge resistance and one exponential in the bead temperature, with one thermal coefficient per family. The same property explains why the cross-ratio of four measured reflection coefficients, invariant under any state-independent two-port, departs from that of the four bridge resistances.
item.dc:creator: Patricio Greco

item.title: Single-Pulse Dosimetry for Ultra-High-Dose-Rate X-Ray Pulses Based on Radiation-Induced Acoustic Signals
item.description: arXiv:2611.27772v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-time dosimetry of ultra-high-dose-rate (UHDR) pulsed X-rays remains a major challenge. This proof-of-principle study investigates a dosimetry method for UHDR pulsed X-rays based on radiation-induced acoustic (RA) signals from a thin metal foil. The foil combines efficient X-ray absorption and acoustic resonance, converting deposited dose into acoustic signals with discrete resonant frequencies. Single-pulse measurements were performed at six dose levels spanning approximately 1--40 mGy(Si), with one pulse recorded at each level and instantaneous dose rates reaching the order of 10^6 Gy/s at the highest dose settings. The peak-to-peak amplified transducer-output voltage exhibited a linear relationship with the reference dose measured by thermoluminescent dosimeters (TLDs). These results demonstrate the feasibility of single-pulse acoustic dosimetry under the tested conditions. Furthermore, we establish analytical solutions for radiation-induced acoustic signals in a one-dimensional layered medium in both the time and frequency domains, providing a theoretical basis for signal interpretation and detector optimization.
item.dc:creator: Qihang Han, Ke Chen, Chenghao Hua, Haoran Chen, Lili Ding, Changhui Li, Xiaoping Ouyang, Chenhui Wang, Wei Chen, Wenjun Ma

item.title: Coherence Lengths of Laser Pointers
item.description: arXiv:2611.26878v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We report on the coherence lengths of low-cost green laser pointers in the midst of multimodal behavior using an optical interferometer based on noncollinear beam geometries and a CMOS detector array. Examined devices include three diode lasers and a frequency-doubled neodymium-emission diode-pumped solid state (DPSS) laser. Coherence length measurements are variable among devices, but values can nevertheless regularly exceed 10 cm. The work serves as a template for an advanced undergraduate physics laboratory experiment and may inspire new kinds of laser pointer devices utilizing interference effects as operative principles.

item.title: 60-cm-long In-vacuum Zerodur Optical Cavity for Optical Lattice Atom Interferometry
item.description: arXiv:2611.27328v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Optical cavities are widely used in atomic physics experiments to control the spatial geometry and spectral properties of atom-light interactions. Recently, an optical lattice generated by the pristine mode of an optical cavity was utilized to hold and extend the quantum coherence of atomic spatial superpositions. Here, we describe an in-vacuum optical cavity designed to enhance the spatial and temporal coherence of optical lattice atom interferometers to one millimeter wavepacket separations and one minute measurement durations. The cavity uses a rigid Zerodur spacer to suppress the negative effects of thermal drift and mechanical-acoustic vibrations on the atomic motional state. The 60 cm-long cavity spacer provides ample optical access for the laser beams and imaging optics necessary for the preparation, quantum control, and read-out of the atomic state, as well as room for various source mass configurations for localized gravitational measurements. An integrated differential pumping structure enables compatibility with ultrahigh-vacuum operation and optical interferometry allows for in-situ vibration monitoring. The performance of the optical cavity is methodically characterized: we measure mirror vibration noise with amplitude below 5 nm/$\sqrt{\rm Hz}$ in a wide frequency range of 2 Hz - 100 kHz and a slow 15 MHz thermal drift of the cavity resonance over 47 hours, which can be readily stabilized with an integrated piezo. The optical cavity supports both 852-nm light for Raman transitions and 1064-nm light for the optical lattice, with a free spectral range matched to an integer divisor of the cesium ground-state hyperfine splitting.
item.dc:creator: Philip Wondrak, Paola Luna, Kenneth Nakasone, Andrei Zhukov, Michael Grisham, Garrett D. Cole, Po-han Chen, Cristian D. Panda

item.title: Optimizing MHz X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy with burst-mode free-electron laser operation
item.description: arXiv:2611.27364v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Burst-mode X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) provide a powerful platform for X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) experiments with sub-microsecond temporal resolution, but the achievable performance is constrained in practice by both photon statistics and the sample's dose tolerance. Here, we develop an analytical framework for estimating the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of pulsed XPCS measurements, including pulse-to-pulse fluctuations of the incident intensity. We combine this description with dose constraints and show that, for a fixed maximum dose, acquiring fewer frames at higher per-pulse intensity yields a higher SNR than distributing the dose over a larger number of low-intensity frames. The framework is validated against measurements at the European XFEL, where the intensity fluctuations of the investigated operation mode are found to cause only a negligible reduction in SNR. We further introduce and experimentally demonstrate a rolling bunch pattern with three pulses per train and variable pulse spacings. This scheme enables more than an order-of-magnitude increase in the accessible per-pulse intensity while maintaining equilibrium dynamics. Our results provide practical guidelines for optimizing dose-efficient MHz-XPCS experiments and for evaluating future XFEL operation modes.

item.title: Experimental and Monte Carlo Simulation Studies to Characterize a Low-Pressure Gas-Based Positive-Ion Detector with a Nanometer-Equivalent Sensitive Volume
item.description: arXiv:2512.11126v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Compact low-pressure gas-based positive-ion detectors offer a promising approach to measuring particle track structure at the nanometer scale. These detectors use electric fields to collect and multiply positive ions produced by the incident radiation in mm-sized holes in dielectric materials, achieving a nm-equivalent spatial resolution of the localization of ionization events when scaled to liquid water at unit density. In this work, a detector prototype featuring a 1.5 mm-diameter hole in a dielectric plate was experimentally characterized. Ion collection and multiplication were achieved by applying a negative high potential to the glass cathode 0.5~mm below the hole, assisted by a low drift field above the plate. A grounded readout electrode with a 0.8 mm hole covers the hole to prevent interactions of collected ions with the hole walls. The experimental setup was further modeled with Geant4-DNA and Garfield++ for deeper insight. By combining the measurements with the Monte Carlo simulations, a per-ion signal formation probability in the low single-digit percentage range was determined. Further, the signal formation mechanism, commonly attributed to ion-impact ionization within the hole, was critically examined. Ion-induced secondary electron emission from surfaces was considered a possible contributor to, or the primary mechanism of, signal formation that has not been addressed in detail in previous studies of this detector concept. Despite the extensive measurements and simulations, the available evidence did not reveal which physical processes governed signal formation or whether either mechanism dominates. We discuss key limitations in the current understanding of this detector class and propose future targeted measurements and simulations to clarify the signal formation mechanism and guide the development of compact positive-ion detectors and nanodosimeters.

item.title: Impact of Environmental Stress on Low Gain Avalanche Diode Sensors Response
item.description: arXiv:2608.22482v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Low Gain Avalanche Diodes or LGADs are silicon sensors capable of achieving excellent timing resolution due to their characteristic internal gain. Detectors based on LGAD technology play a crucial role in High Energy and Nuclear Physics experiments, among other applications. However, their performance is affected by environmental factors such as temperature, humidity, and storage conditions. A systematic evaluation of the response of LGAD sensors as a function of these environmental parameters is therefore of essential importance for any application. LGAD sensors fabricated at the Brookhaven National Laboratory are characterized and stress-tested against various operating conditions, such as rapid temperature and humidity changes. Dedicated and detailed simulations are used to interpret the experimental results.
item.dc:creator: Mohamed Hijas Mohamed Farook, Gaetano Barone, Diallo Boye, Gabriele D'Amen, Gabriele Giacomini, Timo Peltola, Jennifer Roloff, Enrico Rossi, Trevor Russell, Sally Seidel, Alessandro Tricoli, Lixing Wang

item.title: Long-Term Stable Three-Axis Single-Beam Alignment-Based Atomic Magnetometer Using an Uncoated Buffer-Gas-Free Rubidium Ampoule for Unshielded Geomagnetic Monitoring
item.description: arXiv:2611.12905v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Optically pumped magnetometers achieve exceptional sensitivity, yet sustaining long-term baseline stability in unshielded Earth-field environments (~50,000 nT) remains challenging. We present the design, quantum-interference principles, calibration, and unshielded validation of a three-axis single-beam alignment-based atomic magnetometer built from an unmodified, uncoated, buffer-gas-free commercial rubidium (Rb) ampoule and a single 795 nm VCSEL. Pumped with $45^\circ$-oriented linearly polarized light on the $^{87}$Rb $D_1$ ($F=2 \to F'=1$) transition, the sensor exploits ground-state Zeeman quantum interference (rank-2 spin alignment), intrinsically cancelling first-order vector light shifts. Dual-zone 20 kHz AC heating ($75.0^\circ$C lower liquid Rb reservoir, $85.0^\circ$C upper optical zone) suppresses window condensation and thermal magnetic gradients over 29 days. Without buffer-gas pressure broadening, the VCSEL is stabilized via direct absorption spectroscopy at an optimized 3530 Hz dither frequency, eliminating odd-harmonic intermodulation leakage. A hybrid balanced polarimeter extracts $B_x$, $B_y$, and laser-lock errors from total absorption (sum channel) and $B_z$ from alignment-induced linear dichroism (difference channel) within an active zero-field compensation loop using a 12-bit microcontroller in a dual-stage mid-ranging architecture. Spectral analysis yields sub-LSB noise amplitudes of 0.5-5 pT at 1 Hz (15-150 $\mathrm{pT}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$), rolling off to 0.1-1 pT (3-30 $\mathrm{pT}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$) near 10 Hz. Continuous unshielded geomagnetic monitoring in Okayama benchmarked against synthesized Kakioka and Kanoya observatory records demonstrates high tracking fidelity and bounds instrumental bias instability to $\le 0.1$ nT at 100-200 s integration times.
item.dc:creator: Minaru Kawamura
